briefing.ai_skill_help: How quickly and well enemy captains react, evade and coordinate. The AI never receives information its own sensors have not gathered.
class.ijn_bb_kongo.history: Designed in Britain as battlecruisers in 1911 and twice rebuilt into fast battleships. On 13 November 1942 Hiei, sent to bombard Henderson Field with incendiary shells, ran into a US cruiser force at point-blank range; crippled, she was sunk by aircraft the next day. Kirishima was lost to Washington two nights later.
class.ijn_bb_kongo.tactics: Fast and heavily armed but thinly armoured for a battleship. Bombardment shells loaded for a shore target are of little use against ships - change to armour-piercing early.
class.ijn_ca_aoba.history: Aoba and Kinugasa were improved Furutakas with twin turrets. Both fought at Savo; at Cape Esperance in October 1942 Aoba was ambushed by radar-directed US cruisers and badly damaged, Kinugasa was sunk at Guadalcanal in November.
class.ijn_ca_furutaka.history: Japan's first generation of heavy cruisers, small but well armed. Kako was torpedoed by the submarine S-44 on 10 August 1942 while returning from Savo; Furutaka was sunk at Cape Esperance two months later.
class.ijn_ca_takao.history: The Takao class combined ten 20 cm guns with a towering bridge that housed the most elaborate fire-control and command spaces of any cruiser of her time. Chokai was Mikawa's flagship at Savo Island and was hit several times by Quincy's last salvoes.
class.ijn_ca_takao.tactics: Heavy gun and torpedo armament, excellent night optics. Keep the range short at night where its torpedoes and trained lookouts dominate.
class.ijn_cl_nagara.history: The 5,500-ton light cruisers led the destroyer squadrons. Nagara led Abe's screen at the First Naval Battle of Guadalcanal and Kondo's at the second.
class.ijn_cl_sendai.history: The last and most refined of the 5,500-ton cruisers, recognisable by their four funnels. Sendai led the sweeping force around Savo Island on 14 November 1942.
class.ijn_cl_tenryu.history: Small light cruisers of 1919, designed as destroyer flotilla leaders. Old and lightly armed, they were still useful in night actions thanks to their torpedoes.
class.ijn_cl_yubari.history: An experimental design that packed a full light cruiser armament onto a 3,000-ton hull. Yubari fought at Savo Island at the end of Mikawa's column.
class.ijn_dd_akatsuki.history: The last group of the Special Type destroyers. Akatsuki illuminated Atlanta with her searchlight at the start of the First Naval Battle of Guadalcanal and was sunk within minutes.
class.ijn_dd_akizuki.history: Large destroyers built around eight 10 cm high-velocity dual-purpose guns to escort carriers. Teruzuki was brand new at the First Naval Battle of Guadalcanal and was sunk by a PT boat a month later.
class.ijn_dd_asashio.history: The first destroyers built after the treaty limits fell away, forerunners of the Kagero class. Asagumo fought in both naval battles of Guadalcanal in November 1942.
class.ijn_dd_fubuki.history: The 'Special Type' destroyers of 1928 shocked other navies with six 12.7 cm guns in enclosed mounts and nine 61 cm torpedo tubes with reloads. Ayanami fought alone against two US battleships off Savo in November 1942.
class.ijn_dd_kagero.history: The backbone of the 'Tokyo Express' supply runs to Guadalcanal. At Tassafaronga on 30 November 1942 Kagero-class destroyers turned a surprise attack by a superior US cruiser force into a Japanese victory with a mass torpedo launch.
class.ijn_dd_kagero.tactics: Fire torpedoes first, guns second. Reload at sea and attack again. Turn away immediately after launching.
class.ijn_dd_kamikaze.history: Destroyers of the early 1920s. Yunagi accompanied Mikawa to Savo Island and covered the withdrawal.
class.ijn_dd_shiratsuyu.history: The first Japanese destroyers with quadruple torpedo mounts. Yudachi caused havoc in the first naval battle of Guadalcanal; Shigure became famous as a lucky ship.
class.ijn_dd_yugumo.history: Improved Kageros with higher-angle guns. Takanami was lost at Tassafaronga after drawing the fire of the entire US force.
class.ran_ca_kent.history: A British 'County' class treaty cruiser with high freeboard and long range, built for imperial trade protection rather than close combat. HMAS Canberra was hit by more than twenty shells and two torpedoes in the first minutes at Savo Island and had to be scuttled.
class.ran_dd_scott.history: A First World War flotilla leader, lent to Australia with the old destroyers that Axis propaganda mocked as the 'Scrap Iron Flotilla' - a name their crews adopted with pride. Old and worn, HMAS Stuart fought through the whole Mediterranean campaign of 1940-41; at Matapan she engaged Zara and the destroyer Alfieri at close range.
class.rm_ca_zara.history: Italy's best-protected treaty cruisers: the designers saved weight wherever they could to give them a 150 mm belt, more armour than any other cruiser of the treaty generation. Their 203 mm guns were powerful but scattered badly, because both barrels of a turret shared one cradle. On the night of 28 March 1941 Zara and Fiume were sent back to help the crippled Pola - with their guns trained fore and aft they met three British battleships at 3,000 m and were sunk together with Pola.
class.rm_ca_zara.tactics: Strong armour for a cruiser and long-range guns: fight in daylight and at long range. At night keep away from heavy ships - you have no radar and no flashless powder, and your main armament has not trained for it.
class.rm_dd_oriani.history: The last of a line of Italian destroyers derived from the Maestrale class: fast, with two twin 120 mm turrets and two triple torpedo mounts, but lightly built. At Matapan Alfieri and Carducci were sunk covering the cruisers; Oriani escaped damaged and Gioberti unharmed.
class.rn_bb_queen_elizabeth.history: The first fast battleships: oil-fired, eight 15-inch guns and 24 knots in 1915. Warspite, damaged at Jutland, was rebuilt from 1934 to 1937 with new machinery, a tower bridge, longer-ranged guns and thicker decks; Valiant and Queen Elizabeth were rebuilt even more thoroughly, Barham and Malaya only in part. At Cape Matapan Warspite, Valiant and Barham wrecked two Italian heavy cruisers at point-blank range within minutes.
class.rn_bb_queen_elizabeth.tactics: Slow, but heavily armed and armoured. At night let the destroyers and the radar find the enemy, close to point-blank range unseen and open fire together on searchlight illumination: a 15-inch broadside wrecks a cruiser.
class.rn_dd_g.history: The standard British fleet destroyer of the late 1930s: four single 4.7-inch guns and two quadruple torpedo mounts on a handy hull. Greyhound's searchlight picked out Fiume for the battleships' first broadside at Matapan; Havock helped to sink the destroyer Carducci.
class.rn_dd_j.history: Mountbatten's Kelly and her sisters introduced longitudinal framing and the single large funnel to British destroyers, with six 4.7-inch guns and ten torpedo tubes. Jervis led the 14th Flotilla at Matapan; after midnight she took off survivors and torpedoed the burning Zara and the abandoned Pola.
class.rn_dd_tribal.history: Large destroyers built to answer the big Japanese and Italian designs: eight 4.7-inch guns in four twin mounts but only four torpedo tubes - gun ships rather than torpedo boats. Sixteen served in the Royal Navy and twelve were lost. Nubian and Mohawk joined the hunt for the crippled Italian cruisers after Matapan; Mohawk was sunk off Sfax three weeks later.
class.usn_ap_transport.history: Converted liners and freighters that carried the Marines to Guadalcanal. Their protection was the reason the cruisers stood guard around Savo Island.
class.usn_bb_north_carolina.history: The first US battleships built after the naval treaties, armed with nine 16-inch guns and twenty 5-inch/38s. On the night of 14/15 November 1942 Washington, guided by her SG radar, wrecked the battleship Kirishima in seven minutes at about 8,000 yards - the only time a US battleship sank an enemy battleship in a gun duel.
class.usn_bb_north_carolina.tactics: Radar-directed main battery outranges anything the enemy can show at night. Keep the destroyers ahead as a screen and open fire before the enemy's searchlights find you.
class.usn_bb_south_dakota.history: A shorter, more heavily protected design with a single funnel. At the Second Naval Battle of Guadalcanal South Dakota lost all electrical power at the critical moment, was illuminated and hit 26 times - but survived while Washington destroyed Kirishima.
class.usn_ca_new_orleans.history: The last US 'treaty' heavy cruisers, with better armour than their predecessors. Astoria, Quincy and Vincennes were all sunk at Savo Island - surprised, illuminated by searchlights and shot to pieces before they could reply effectively.
class.usn_ca_new_orleans.tactics: Strong gun platform. Do not let the enemy close at night unseen: keep crews at battle stations near enemy waters and use radar early.
class.usn_ca_northampton.history: Northampton-class cruisers carried nine 8-inch guns in three triple turrets. USS Chicago lost her bow to a torpedo at Savo and failed to warn the northern group; Northampton herself was sunk by Long Lance torpedoes at Tassafaronga.
class.usn_ca_pensacola.history: The first US treaty cruisers, with ten 8-inch guns but thin armour. Salt Lake City fought at Cape Esperance; Pensacola survived a Long Lance hit at Tassafaronga.
class.usn_ca_portland.history: Two improved Northamptons. Portland lost her stern steering to a torpedo off Guadalcanal on 13 November 1942, circled helplessly - and still fired six salvos into the crippled Hiei.
class.usn_cl_atlanta.history: Built as anti-aircraft cruisers and destroyer leaders, with sixteen 5-inch/38 guns and torpedo tubes but very light armour. Atlanta was wrecked by a torpedo and by gunfire - partly from San Francisco - at the First Naval Battle of Guadalcanal; Juneau was sunk by a submarine as she withdrew.
class.usn_cl_brooklyn.history: Fifteen rapid-firing 6-inch guns gave the Brooklyns a tremendous volume of fire at short and medium range. Boise was badly hit at Cape Esperance after illuminating a target with her searchlight.
class.usn_cl_brooklyn.tactics: Volume of fire, not penetration: overwhelm cruisers and destroyers at 8-12 km. Avoid searchlights - they mark you for every enemy gun.
class.usn_cl_st_louis.history: A refined Brooklyn with 5-inch/38 dual-purpose guns. USS Helena's SG surface radar gave the first warning at Cape Esperance - the turning point of radar in night actions.
class.usn_dd_bagley.history: Destroyers with sixteen torpedo tubes. Blue and Ralph Talbot were the radar pickets that failed to detect Mikawa at Savo; Bagley and Patterson screened the southern group.
class.usn_dd_benson.history: Benson/Gleaves-class destroyers formed many of the screens in the Solomons. Laffey fought at point-blank range against the battleship Hiei in November 1942.
class.usn_dd_fletcher.history: The definitive US destroyer of the war: five 5-inch/38 guns, ten torpedo tubes and good radar. Fletcher herself fought at Guadalcanal and Tassafaronga.
class.usn_dd_mahan.history: Mid-1930s destroyers with twelve torpedo tubes. Cushing led the US column into the first naval battle of Guadalcanal.

credits.game_text: A tactical naval simulation of surface warfare in the Second World War. Design, simulation, artificial intelligence, procedural models and engine were created for this project.
credits.history_text: Ship and weapon data use commonly published figures, rounded and simplified for play. Further reading: NavWeaps (navweaps.com), Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships 1922-1946, S. E. Morison 'History of United States Naval Operations in World War II' vol. V, R. Lundgren 'The World Wonder'd', J. D. Hornfischer 'Neptune's Inferno'.

scenario.cape_esperance.briefing: Night of 11/12 October 1942, off Cape Esperance, the north-western tip of Guadalcanal. To cover a convoy bringing Army reinforcements to the Marines, Rear Admiral Norman Scott's Task Group 64.2 - the heavy cruisers San Francisco and Salt Lake City, the light cruisers Boise and Helena and five destroyers - waits between Savo Island and the cape. Rear Admiral Aritomo Gotō is coming down 'the Slot' with the heavy cruisers Aoba, Furutaka and Kinugasa and two destroyers to shell Henderson Field, while a separate Japanese group lands troops and artillery further along the coast. The moon has set, the sky is overcast, the sea calm.
scenario.cape_esperance.history: Helena's SG radar found Gotō's force at about 23:25, but the report reached Scott only as his column was countermarching, and the van destroyers ended up between the two forces. Even so the Americans crossed the Japanese 'T'. At 23:46 Helena opened fire without waiting for orders and the others followed. Gotō, convinced he was being fired on by friendly ships, turned away too late and was mortally wounded on Aoba's bridge. Furutaka and the destroyer Fubuki were sunk and Aoba badly damaged. The Americans lost Duncan, caught between both lines; Farenholt was hit by friendly shells, and Boise survived a magazine fire only because the sea flooding in through a shell hole put it out. It was the US Navy's first victory in a night surface action - yet the Japanese reinforcements were landed all the same.
scenario.cape_esperance.intel_allies: Search aircraft reported Japanese cruisers and destroyers coming down the Slot at high speed this afternoon. Expect them off Savo Island around midnight. Against cruisers the SG radar reaches about 25 km.
scenario.cape_esperance.intel_axis: Air reconnaissance found only American cruisers and destroyers far to the south of Guadalcanal. Our own reinforcement group is unloading off the coast tonight - ships sighted near Savo may well be friendly.
scenario.cape_esperance.orders_allies: Intercept the Japanese force west of Savo Island before it can shell Henderson Field. Your crews have trained for exactly this night action and are at battle stations. Helena and Boise carry the new SG search radar - use it, but keep the column together: identification at night is uncertain and your own destroyers steam ahead of the cruisers.
scenario.cape_esperance.orders_axis: Take the bombardment group past Savo Island, shell Henderson Field and withdraw to the north-west before dawn. No American surface ships are expected - they have not contested these waters at night since August. Your crews are at cruising stations, the guns trained fore and aft.
scenario.cape_esperance.title: Battle of Cape Esperance
scenario.cape_matapan.briefing: Night of 28 March 1941, south-west of Cape Matapan, the southern tip of Greece. All day Admiral Cunningham's Mediterranean Fleet has chased Admiral Iachino's fleet westwards. In the afternoon torpedo bombers from HMS Formidable hit the battleship Vittorio Veneto, and at dusk another torpedo stopped the heavy cruiser Pola dead in the water. Believing the British battleships far away, Iachino has sent the cruisers Zara and Fiume and four destroyers back to help her. Cunningham, with Warspite, Valiant and Barham and four destroyers, is steering west towards the place where Pola lies. The sea is calm, the night dark.
scenario.cape_matapan.history: Valiant's radar found the stopped Pola shortly after 22:00. Minutes later the destroyer Stuart sighted large ships crossing ahead: Zara and Fiume with their destroyers, completely unaware. At 22:27 Greyhound switched on her searchlight, and Warspite, Valiant and Barham fired full broadsides at under 4 km. Fiume sank within the hour; Zara was left burning and was finished by Jervis's torpedoes in the early morning. The destroyers Alfieri and Carducci were sunk as they counter-attacked. Jervis and Nubian took off Pola's crew and sank her at about 04:00. Some 2,300 Italian sailors died; the British lost a single aircraft. After Matapan the Italian battle fleet rarely ventured into the eastern Mediterranean again.
scenario.cape_matapan.intel_allies: Aircraft reported the enemy battleship damaged and slowing. Shortly after dark the cruiser Ajax's radar found a large ship lying stopped some six miles off her track. More enemy cruisers may be in the area.
scenario.cape_matapan.intel_axis: Air reconnaissance this afternoon reported an aircraft carrier and battleships, but the staff believes them far to the east. Nothing indicates a British force close by. None of our ships carries radar.
scenario.cape_matapan.orders_allies: Find the stopped enemy cruiser and destroy whatever comes to her aid. Valiant's Type 279 radar can find a cruiser at about 11 km. Let the destroyers lead, close to point-blank range unseen, illuminate with searchlights and open fire with all three battleships together. The 14th Flotilla (Jervis) is returning from the hunt for Vittorio Veneto and will join later in the night.
scenario.cape_matapan.orders_axis: Return to the stopped Pola with Zara, Fiume and the 9th Destroyer Division, take her in tow or take off her crew, and rejoin the fleet. The enemy battle fleet is believed to be far to the east; at most light forces may be about. Your heavy guns are secured fore and aft and the crews are at cruising stations - night action is not part of your training.
scenario.cape_matapan.title: Battle of Cape Matapan
scenario.first_guadalcanal.briefing: Friday, 13 November 1942, 01:25, Ironbottom Sound. Vice Admiral Hiroaki Abe is coming down past Savo Island with the battleships Hiei and Kirishima, the light cruiser Nagara and eleven destroyers. His magazines are topped with incendiary shells: tonight he is to burn Henderson Field, so that a convoy of eleven transports can land 7,000 soldiers tomorrow. In his way stands Rear Admiral Daniel Callaghan with what was left after escorting the day's supply ships: two heavy and three light cruisers and eight destroyers in one long column. There are no American battleships within reach. The night is moonless, rain squalls hang over the sound - and neither side quite knows where the other is.
scenario.first_guadalcanal.history: Helena's radar found the Japanese at 01:24, but the American column ran on while its admiral asked for bearings over a crowded radio net. The two forces blundered into each other; at 01:50 Akatsuki switched on her searchlight and the most confused surface action of the war began at ranges of a few hundred metres. Atlanta was shot to pieces and torpedoed, Admiral Scott killed on her bridge; San Francisco took 14-inch shells and Callaghan died with his staff. Hiei, hit by some 85 shells, lost her steering and circled north of Savo - aircraft from Henderson Field sank her the next day. The Americans lost Atlanta, Juneau (torpedoed by a submarine the next morning) and four destroyers; the Japanese lost Hiei, Akatsuki and Yudachi. Abe turned back without firing a shell at the airfield, and the convoy's landing had to be postponed.
scenario.first_guadalcanal.intel_allies: Search planes reported two battleships or heavy cruisers, a cruiser and up to a dozen destroyers coming down the Slot this afternoon. Expect them off Savo Island after midnight, heading for Lunga Point.
scenario.first_guadalcanal.intel_axis: During the day American transports unloaded off Lunga Point, covered by cruisers and destroyers. The transports have left; whether their escort is still in the sound is unknown. Our lookouts will have to find them - none of our ships carries radar.
scenario.first_guadalcanal.orders_allies: Stop the bombardment force before it reaches Lunga Point. Henderson Field must not be shelled tonight - whatever it costs. You are outgunned: the enemy battleships carry 14-inch guns, your heaviest are 8-inch. Close the range, fight at night where their guns matter less, and use your destroyers' torpedoes. Helena, O'Bannon and Fletcher carry the new SG radar - the flagship San Francisco does not.
scenario.first_guadalcanal.orders_axis: Take the raiding group past Savo Island to Lunga Point and bombard Henderson Field: the battleships must stay at least ten minutes within 7 km of the airfield. Withdraw to the north-west by 03:00 at the latest. If American warships bar the way, the destroyers attack with torpedoes first, as the doctrine demands.
scenario.first_guadalcanal.title: First Naval Battle of Guadalcanal
scenario.savo_island.briefing: Night of 8/9 August 1942, Ironbottom Sound off Guadalcanal. Two days ago US Marines landed on Guadalcanal and Tulagi; the transports are still unloading off Lunga Point. Vice Admiral Gunichi Mikawa has raced down from Rabaul with five heavy cruisers, two light cruisers and a destroyer. The Allied screen is split around Savo Island: a southern group (HMAS Canberra, USS Chicago and two destroyers), a northern group (Vincennes, Quincy, Astoria and two destroyers) and two radar pickets west of the island. The night is dark and overcast, rain squalls drift over the sound, the moon has set.
scenario.savo_island.history: Historically Mikawa's column slipped past the picket destroyers unseen. Floatplanes dropped flares over the southern group; within minutes Canberra was wrecked by gunfire and Chicago lost her bow to a torpedo, without warning the northern group. Mikawa swept around Savo and destroyed Vincennes, Quincy and Astoria in close-range night action. More than a thousand Allied sailors died. Fearing air attack at dawn, Mikawa withdrew without attacking the transports; on the way home Kako was sunk by the submarine S-44. It remains one of the heaviest defeats ever suffered by the US Navy.
scenario.savo_island.intel_allies: A sighting by an Australian Hudson on 8 August reported 'three cruisers, three destroyers and two seaplane tenders' heading south-east - read as a force setting up a seaplane base. The report arrived hours late. No surface attack is expected tonight.
scenario.savo_island.intel_axis: Reconnaissance on 7 August reported several cruisers and destroyers covering the landing. Expect patrol lines on both sides of Savo Island; destroyers with radar may be posted to the west.
scenario.savo_island.orders_allies: Guard both entrances to the anchorage around Savo Island and stop any surface force before it reaches the transports. Your crews have been at action stations for two days and are now in Condition II - raising the alarm will cost precious minutes. Radar (SC on the destroyers) is unreliable close to land.
scenario.savo_island.orders_axis: Pass Savo Island undetected, destroy the Allied cruisers in a night action and, if possible, strike the transports off Lunga Point. Break off in time: by daylight you must be out of range of American carrier aircraft. Japanese night training, Type 93 torpedoes and surprise are your weapons.
scenario.savo_island.title: Battle of Savo Island
scenario.second_guadalcanal.briefing: Night of 14/15 November 1942, 22:55, south of Savo Island. Two nights after Abe's failure, Vice Admiral Nobutake Kondō is bringing the battleship Kirishima, the heavy cruisers Atago and Takao, two light cruisers and nine destroyers to finish the job: Henderson Field is to be shelled so that Tanaka's battered transports can beach at dawn. This time the Americans have battleships of their own. Rear Admiral Willis Lee, the Navy's foremost radar expert, has brought Washington and South Dakota - new, fast and armed with 16-inch guns - and four destroyers scraped together from different units. Lee's ships have rounded Savo and are steaming west, south of the island. A light breeze, a first-quarter moon low in the west, scattered showers.
scenario.second_guadalcanal.history: Washington's radar found Sendai at 23:00, and at 23:17 both battleships opened fire at 15 km - Sendai turned away behind smoke without a hit. Minutes later the American destroyers met the Japanese screen coming round Savo: against the dark island they were seen first, and Japanese torpedoes and gunfire sank Walke and Preston, crippled Benham and set Gwin on fire. South Dakota lost all electrical power at the worst moment, stumbled towards the Japanese main body and was caught in their searchlights; 27 shells wrecked her upper works. Washington, still unseen, opened fire on Kirishima at 7.7 km around midnight - nine 16-inch hits left the Japanese battleship burning and unmanageable, and she was scuttled at 03:25. Dozens of Long Lances fired at Washington all missed. Kondo withdrew, Henderson Field was not shelled, and the transports that beached at Tassafaronga at dawn were destroyed from the air. It was the last time the Japanese tried to win Guadalcanal with their battleships.
scenario.second_guadalcanal.intel_allies: Submarines and search planes have tracked a force of battleships or cruisers and many destroyers coming south all afternoon. Expect it off Savo Island before midnight. The transports Tanaka is escorting are still north of the island.
scenario.second_guadalcanal.intel_axis: Air reconnaissance this afternoon reported two cruisers and four destroyers south of Guadalcanal, steaming north. They may be in the sound tonight. (The pilots were wrong: the 'cruisers' were battleships.)
scenario.second_guadalcanal.orders_allie: Stop Kondo's bombardment force. Your battleships' radar sees far beyond any Japanese lookout, and your 16-inch guns outrange everything they have - but fire at night by radar alone is still guesswork at long range, and in these narrow waters their destroyers can come at you out of the shadow of Savo Island with torpedoes you cannot see. Keep the destroyers ahead as a screen and do not let the battleships be ambushed.
scenario.second_guadalcanal.orders_axis: Bombard Henderson Field with the main body: Kirishima, Atago and Takao must stay ten minutes within 7 km of the airfield; withdraw by 01:30. Sendai's sweeping unit scouts east of Savo and reports; Nagara's screening unit goes round the west of the island and clears the way. Any enemy found is attacked with torpedoes first.
scenario.second_guadalcanal.title: Second Naval Battle of Guadalcanal
scenario.tassafaronga.briefing: Night of 30 November 1942, off Tassafaronga Point on the north coast of Guadalcanal. Rear Admiral Raizō Tanaka's Destroyer Squadron 2 - eight destroyers - is running the 'Tokyo Express': six of them carry drums of food and supplies lashed on deck, to be dropped off the coast and hauled ashore by the starving garrison. To make room, the drum ships left their reload torpedoes behind. Rear Admiral Carleton Wright, in command of Task Force 67 for only two days, is coming in through Lengo Channel with four heavy cruisers, a light cruiser and six destroyers to stop them. The night is very dark and the sea calm; against the jungle-covered shore the Japanese ships are almost invisible.
scenario.tassafaronga.history: American radar picked up the Japanese at about 23:06, but Wright hesitated before releasing his destroyers' torpedoes; when they were finally fired the range had opened and none hit. The cruisers' gunfire fell mostly on Takanami, the nearest Japanese ship, which was wrecked and sunk. Tanaka's other destroyers turned away and launched more than forty torpedoes without firing a gun. Minutes later Minneapolis, New Orleans, Pensacola and Northampton were hit: Minneapolis and New Orleans lost their bows, Pensacola burned for hours, and Northampton sank after midnight. One Japanese destroyer lost against one heavy cruiser sunk and three crippled - Tassafaronga became a textbook example of the torpedo tactics of the IJN, even though no supplies were landed that night.
scenario.tassafaronga.intel_allies: Coast watchers and radio intelligence predict a run of eight destroyers, possibly with transports, to Guadalcanal tonight. Expect them along the coast off Tassafaronga around 23:00.
scenario.tassafaronga.intel_axis: American cruisers and destroyers have been seen in the area during the last days; their position tonight is unknown. Expect to be opposed. None of our ships carries radar.
scenario.tassafaronga.orders_allies: Intercept the Tokyo Express off Tassafaronga and destroy it. The plan: the van destroyers attack first with radar-aimed torpedoes, then the cruisers open fire at about 11 km. Your SG radars see the enemy long before any lookout - the Japanese have no radar, but they have the most dangerous torpedoes afloat.
scenario.tassafaronga.orders_axis: Reach the drop point off Tassafaronga, release the supply drums and withdraw to the north-west. Avoid action if you can - but if enemy cruisers appear, your crews know what to do: turn away, launch the Type 93s unseen and let the torpedoes do the work.
scenario.tassafaronga.title: Battle of Tassafaronga

torpedo.ijn_type93.note: The 'Long Lance': a 61 cm oxygen-fuelled torpedo with enormous range and a heavy warhead. It leaves almost no wake - at night it arrives unseen. The Allies did not know of its performance in 1942 and kept mistaking torpedo hits for submarine attacks.
torpedo.rm_si_270.note: Italian 53.3 cm torpedo from Silurificio Italiano: very fast at short range, with a lighter warhead than its British and Japanese counterparts.
torpedo.rn_mk9.note: The Royal Navy's destroyer torpedo of the war years: reliable, with a heavy warhead, but leaving a clear wake.
torpedo.usn_mk15.note: The standard US destroyer torpedo. In 1942 its Mark 6 exploder and depth control were unreliable: many hits failed to explode or the torpedoes ran too deep.
